Maladaptive Strategies.value: never allow myself to feel or express anger
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
issues.explanation: For trauma involving a child's life-threatening illness, revenge-focused ideation about identifiable responsible people is hard to reconcile unless there was clear culpability (e.g. negligence), which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It appears clinically mismatched to the stated trauma context.

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: Generalized threat from strangers and scanning faces for danger fit interpersonal assault or public violence better than a child's medical crisis. These threat items imply fear of hostile people in ordinary situations, but the rest of the profile does not provide a coherent bridge from the illness trauma to stranger-based danger expectations.

issues.item: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
issues.explanation: Intense rage on recall could occur, but here it primarily supports the revenge item and interpersonal-threat theme. In combination with the stranger-threat items, it pulls the profile toward an assault/perpetrator formulation rather than a child's illness trauma formulation.

issues.item: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me
issues.explanation: Meaning seeking is not inherently maladaptive and, in this profile, sits awkwardly with the otherwise threat-trigger-memory driven formulation; it does not clearly function as an avoidance/safety strategy tied to the selected triggers, threat items, or memory pattern.

issues.item: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance for interpersonal threat in faces/body language is difficult to reconcile with the trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, where danger is more plausibly linked to medical cues, loss cues, or signs of illness rather than hostile people.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: Needing to stay alert to fall asleep implies ongoing external danger monitoring; for a trauma centered on a child's illness, this would usually require clearer linkage to caregiving/medical monitoring, which is absent from the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: For the indexed trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, 'anything that reminds me of someone I have lost' implies bereavement/loss rather than ongoing threat or illness trauma. That is a hard-to-explain mismatch unless the child died, which is not the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: Within the overall profile, the dominant theme is fear/hypervigilance/disorientation around threat cues (sirens, crying, startle, sleep vigilance, physical reactivity, confused/unreal memory). 'Intense rage' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the rest of the profile and sits awkwardly beside suppression of anger, making this item clinically less coherent than the others.

Clinical Vignette: Marco

Marco was twenty-two when his daughter Sofía was born—a moment he had rehearsed a thousand times in his mind, imagining the weight of her in his arms, the way her small fingers would curl around his thumb. He and Sofía's mother had separated before the pregnancy was far along, but Marco had never wavered in his intention to be present, to be the father his own had never been. When Sofía arrived, three weeks early and smaller than expected, Marco took leave from his junior role at the analytics firm and spent eighteen hours a day at the hospital, learning to change her diaper, studying the monitors that beeped softly beside her isolette, memorizing the rhythm of her breathing.

At four months old, Sofía developed a fever that climbed past one hundred and four degrees in a matter of hours. Marco was alone with her when it happened—he was changing her when he noticed her body felt wrong, hot and somehow wrong in a way that made his stomach drop. He called 911 in a state of clarity he would later struggle to reconstruct. What he remembered instead was the siren—the sound of it approaching the apartment, a wail that seemed to split the air itself, and then the paramedics moving with a speed and efficiency that terrified him more than the fever did, because they moved like people who had seen children die before. At the hospital, Sofía spent eight days in the pediatric intensive care unit with bacterial meningitis. Marco did not leave. He sat beside her incubator, watching her small body convulse with seizures, watching her pupils dilate and contract, watching doctors and nurses move in and out with expressions he had learned to read as grave. When she cried—a thin, weak sound that bore no resemblance to her normal cry—he felt something break inside himself that he had not yet found a way to repair.

Sofía recovered. By the time she was discharged, the infection had cleared, and the neurologists said there was no evidence of permanent damage. Marco returned to work after two weeks, and for a time, he told himself the worst was over. But the worst had not ended; it had simply changed shape.

Now, at twenty-five, Marco startle at sounds he barely registers—a car horn, a door slamming, the beep of the microwave in the office kitchen—and his body goes rigid, his heart hammering as though the siren is approaching again. He has not slept through a single night in three years. He lies awake in the dark, listening, alert for any sound that might signal danger, unable to believe that Sofía is safe in her mother's apartment across the city. The conviction that something catastrophic is about to happen sits beneath his ribs like a stone.

What frightened him most was not the memory itself but the fact that he could not hold it steady in his mind. When he tried to recall the sequence of events, they fractured and rearranged themselves. Had the fever come first, or the call to 911? Was the siren before or after the paramedics arrived? The memory felt too extreme, too saturated with terror, and his mind seemed to reject it as though it could not possibly be true—even though he knew, with absolute certainty, that it was. When he allowed himself to remember, the terror returned in full, undiminished, as though no time had passed at all.

He had learned, without consciously deciding to, never to feel angry. Anger felt dangerous, as though it might crack something open. When frustration rose in him—at a slow database query, at a colleague's mistake, at his own helplessness—he forced it down, swallowed it, moved on. He did not cry, not ever, not even alone. Crying felt like losing control, and he could not afford to lose control.

He began avoiding hospitals, ambulances, even his annual physical. He told himself he was fine, that there was no point in medical examinations, that staying away from those places meant staying away from the possibility of catastrophe. At work, his avoidance had begun to cost him. Two months ago, his firm had asked him to present findings to a healthcare client, and Marco had declined without explanation. His manager had not pushed, but Marco could see the concern in his face, the calculation that something was wrong. He had not been promoted last quarter; he suspected it was connected to his withdrawal.

Six weeks ago, Sofía had asked her mother why her papá never came to visit anymore. He did visit—he was careful about that—but perhaps not carefully enough. The question had lodged itself in his chest, and it was still there, a small sharp stone that he could not dislodge. Last week, he had finally called a therapist, not because he believed anything could change, but because he could no longer live as he was living. What he most feared was that the terror would never release him, that he would spend the rest of his life waiting for the next catastrophe. What he hoped for, though he barely dared to articulate it, was that one day he might hold his daughter without his hands shaking.
